forms.title: PATIENT ASSESSMENT, REASSESSMENT AND VITAL SIGNS

items.text: State the nurse's role and responsibility in completing a Comprehensive Patient Assessment, Reassessment and Vital Signs for a patient in area of practice and comparing findings with the patient's baseline findings are so important to overall assessment.
Verbalize the role and responsibilities of the nurse and the need to start the assessment with taking a full Health History, family history, psychosocial history and activities of daily living.
Discuss why assessment involves collecting both subjective and objective data of the presenting complaint.
Explain why observing the patient's body language during assessment is important.

State the PQRSTP model of exploring the chief complaint i.e. Proactive or palliative (provokes or relieves symptoms), quality or quantity (what does symptom/s feel, look or sound like), region or radiation (where is the symptom/s) severity of symptom/s including PAIN SCORE, timing (when was it sudden, how often and how long does symptom/s last), psychosocial history, (find out how the patient feels about himself, his place in society and his relationships with others).

Explain how to properly observe the patient using 'some teams' – symmetry (are face and body symmetrical!?), old (do they look their age?), mentation (are they alert confused agitated or inattentive?), expression (do they appear ill, in pain or anxious?) trunk (are they thin, stocky, obese or barrel-chested?), extremities (are the fingers clubbed, are there joint abnormalities or edema?), appearance (are they clean and appropriately dressed?), movement (is their posture, gait and coordination normal, are they mobile and able to ambulate normally?), speech (is their speech relaxed, clear, strong, understandable and appropriate, do they sound stressed?).
Verbalize the standard for the frequency of measuring vital signs as per policy in area of practice.
Discuss the weight and height, temperature and pain score as vital signs and why these are important.
State how to assess the pulse noting rate, rhythm and strength and why these are important when considering the amount of blood ejected with each heartbeat.
Discuss the rationale for not using the thumb for taking a pulse or blood pressure.
Discuss the limitations of measuring oxygen saturation with pulse oximeter.
State when manual blood pressure readings and pulses are preferable to automated readings.
Explain and calculate the Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) i.e. SBP +2 x DBP/3 and why this is important note.
Explore the observations and parameters for reporting significant findings and vital signs to nurse in charge and/or physician.
Discuss the need and how to document the patient's comprehensive assessment, reassessment and vital signs findings and at the time of completion.

Demonstrate how to complete a comprehensive patient assessment, reassessment and vital signs of a patient in area of practice and compare findings with the patient's baseline results and explain why this comparison data is so important to the overall assessment of the patient and the chief complaint.
Complete an assessment on a patient with taking a full health history e.g. biographic data, chief complaint, medical history, family history, psychosocial history and activities of daily living.
Demonstrate the collecting of both subjective and objective data when completing an assessment.
List and demonstrate some examples of the patient's body language noted during the completion of an assessment and state what message/s the patient might have been communicating.

Demonstrate the use of the PQRST model of exploring the chief complaint i.e. proactive or palliative (provokes or relieves symptoms), quality or quantity (what does symptoms/s feel, look or sound like), region or radiation (where is the symptom/s) severity of symptom/s including PAIN SCORE, timing (when, was it sudden, how often and how does symptom/s last).

Complete an observation of a patient using 'some teams' – symmetry (are face and body symmetrical?), old (do they look their age?) mentation (are they alert, confused agitated or inattentive?), expression (do they appear ill, in pain or anxious?), trunk (are they thin, stocky, obese or barrel-chested?), extremities (are the fingers clubbed, are there joint abnormalities or edema?) appearance (are they clean and appropriately dressed?), movement (is their posture, gait and coordination normal, are they mobile and able to ambulate normally?) Speech (is their speech relaxed, clear, strong, understandable and appropriate, do they sound stressed?).
Complete the documentation for the frequency of measuring vital signs as per policy in area of practice.
Demonstrate taking the weight and height, temperature and pain score as vital signs.
Demonstrate how to assess the pulse noting rate, rhythm and strength and why these are important when considering the amount of blood ejected with each heartbeat.
Complete the measuring of oxygen saturation with pulse oximeter.
Complete both manual blood pressure readings and pulse and automated readings.
Demonstrate how to read and calculate the Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP).
Complete the documentation and reporting of significant findings and vital signs to nurse in charge and/or physician.
Complete the documentation of the patient's comprehensive assessment, reassessment and vital signs accurately.
Accept constructive criticism as learning opportunity/s.
To be self-aware of limitation in knowledge and skills.
To be approachable and open to answer patient and family's questions.

forms.title: EARLY WARNING SIGNS AND SHOCK EMERGENCIES

items.text: Explain the rationale for EARLY WARNING SIGNS i.e. to provide an integrated approach to the recognition and response to 'at risk' patients, preventing avoidable deterioration.
Explore how being aware of EARLY WARNING SIGNS will improve patient outcomes and why this is important in terms of the quality of life.
Explain why real time vital signs are important when a patient is recognized as 'at risk' e.g. initial baseline and on-going trends.
Discuss the EARLY WARNING SIGNS Tool developed for area of practice and explain how the EWS Scale works.

List the NURSING INTERVENTIONS AUTHORIZED once Early Warning Signs are identified and why these are important to patient outcomes
NOTE: Patients hemodynamic status and assess airway, breathing and circulation by repeating VITAL SIGNS at least every 15 minutes.

Explain why it is necessary to ensure that the following items are ready / accessible:
• Crash cart
• Suction equipment
• Oxygen delivery
• IV set up and fluids
• Dynamap with oxygen saturation probe
Define shock i.e. when cells become hypoxic as a result of decreased perfusion.

Discuss the categories and causes of shock:
Hypovolemic – massive external bleeding, hemothorax, fractures, gastrointestinal bleeding, diabetes mellitus insipidus burns, excessive diuretic use, ascites, massive vomiting or diarrhoea
Cardiogenic – MI, cardiomyopathy, cardiac contusion, dysrhythmias, heart valve disease
Distributive – sepsis, anaphylaxis, spinal cord injury, overdose, anoxia
Obstructive – tension pneumothorax, pericardial tamponade, pulmonary embolus, intra-cardiac clot, vena cava clot, aortic aneurysm, aortic stenosis, valvular disease, gravid uterus

Explore the cellular effects of shock e.g. < ATP (adenosine triphosphate), excess lactic acid production, mitochondrial death, cellular oedema, deterioration of the sodium-potassium pump, hyperkalaemia.

Discuss the progression of shock:
• Compensatory – body responses initiated to increase cardiac output, tissue (cellular perfusion) and vital organ perfusion
• Progressive – body responses become inadequate to maintain perfusion and multisystem failure ensues
• Irreversible – pervasive cellular destruction; death is imminent

Explain the rationale for pertinent historical date:
1. Chief Complaint
2. Pain, pressure (PQRST)
• Provocation
• Quality
• Radiation/region
• Severity (scale 0-5 or 0-10)
• Time of onset
3. Level of consciousness
4. Dizziness, syncope
5. Weakness, fatigue
6. Difficulty breathing
7. Edema – location and type
8. Vomiting, hematemesis
9. Diarrhea, melena
10. Vaginal bleeding
11. Fever, chills
12. Rash, urticarial
13. Polyuria, thirst
14. Injury, location, mechanism, force, protective device
15. Bleeding, site, estimated blood loss
16. Medical-surgical history
17. Allergies

Discuss the acid base deviations that occur:
Respiratory Acidosis – Hypoventilation results in CO2 retention, carbonic acid excess and <pH Metabolic Acidosis – Excess fixed acids results in <pH
Respiratory Alkalosis – Hyperventilation results in >CO2 exhaled, reducing carbonic acid with >pH Metabolic Alkalosis – >pH due to excess base or acid deficits

Explore the adverse effects of fluid and/or blood replacement:
1. Hypothermia – transfusion of banked blood without warming can make the patient hypothermic. Hypothermia shifts the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve to the left i.e. oxygen is not available for the cells.
2. Hyperkalemia – lysis of blood cells releases potassium from the intracellular space so the patient becomes hyperkalemic. Monitor the patient's serum potassium and observe for cardiac rhythm problems.
3. Hypocalcaemia – banked blood contains citrate which binds with free calcium. Calcium chloride is given after 10U of blood.
4. Acidosis – the pH of banked blood is 7.1 and with large amounts of banked blood, acidosis can occur. Monitor ABGs and watch for dysrhythmias.
5. Alkalosis – large amounts of banked blood, alkalosis can develop because the citrate is converted by the liver into bicarbonate.
6. Clotting problems – clotting factors are lost in most banked blood. Coagulation times may be prolonged and clotting problems occur with massive blood transfusions. Usually 1U of fresh-frozen plasma is given after 10U of blood.
7. Intravascular debris – banked blood contains debris as a result of processing and therefore blood is always given through a filter.

Demonstrate the patient assessment for Stage 1 of shock:
Stage I – Compensatory
Increased heart rate (101-150 bpm)
Skin: pale, moist, clammy
Pupils: dilated (6-8 mm, react to light appropriately)
Blood pressure: usually normal at this stage
Heart rhythm: sinus tachycardia
Respirations: increased (>24 bpm)
Peripheral pulse: weak
Altered level of consciousness: confused, anxious, restless, lethargic
Glasgow Coma Scale
Poor capillary refill (>2 seconds)
May have petechiae or purpura
Depending on the cause may be at risk for infection
*This is the stage with the best chance of reversibility

Demonstrate the patient assessment for Stage 2 of shock:
Stage II – Progressive
Increased heart rate
Skin: cool, moist, clammy
Pupils: dilated, sluggish response
Blood pressure: starting to drop
Heart rhythm: sinus tachycardia
Respirations: rapid and deep
Altered level of consciousness worsens
Decreased urinary output
Peripheral edema
Dysrhythmias

Demonstrate the patient assessment for Stage 3 of shock:
Stage III - Irreversible
Decreased heart rate
Skin: cold
Pupils: dilated, very sluggish
Severe hypotension
Severe bradycardia
Respiratory failure
Possible coma
Anuria
Peripheral edema
Death

forms.title: PAIN AND DISCOMFORT: PATIENT MANAGEMENT GUIDELINES

items.text: Explain why it is important for a nurse to accept that pain is what the patient says it is, and exist when he/ she says it does.
Discuss the rationale for the World Health Organization making the recommendation that pain is the fifth vital signs.

Explain why it is important for a nurse to pay special attention to Vulnerable Patients when their inability to communicate verbally does not negate the possibility that an individual is experiencing pain and is in need of appropriate pain relieving treatment.

Describe what acute pain is i.e. it has a sudden onset and commonly reduces over the short period of time (days, hours, minutes) and often follows injury to the body and generally disappears when the injury heals.
Describe the objective physical signs associated with acute pain e.g. tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis, mydriasis (dilation of the pupil) and pallor.

Describe the chronic pain is i.e. pain which persists a month beyond the usual course of an acute disease or a reasonable time for an injury to heal, or that is associated with a chronic pathologic process that causes continuous pain or the pain recurs at intervals for month or years.
Describe procedural pain i.e. pain and/ or discomfort from diagnostic or therapeutic procedures, such as lumbar puncture, wound and burn debridement etc.

Describe discomfort i.e. mental or physical uneasiness, including nauseas, which occurs as a result of acute or chronic conditions, diagnostic or therapeutic procedures or anticipation of them, or as side effects of analgesia.

Explain how to complete a full pain assessment i.e.
• Pain intensity
• Location
• Duration
• Character
• Frequency
• Pain score
• Pain relief taken and effect
For vulnerable or patients unable to communicate verbally use the appropriate objective Pain assessment tool (modified FLACC and FRAAC)
1. Adult patient is 14 years and older
2. Pediatric – patient is younger than 14
3. Neonate – patient younger than 40 weeks corrected gestational age, plus 28 days
State the various measures for pain control i.e. pharmacological and non-pharmacological.

Describe the elements of Pain management that patient need to be educated about when it is part of the treatment, such as:
• Understanding Pain and other symptoms
• The risk of Pain and other symptoms
• The importance of effective pain and symptom management
• The assessment process for pain and symptoms
• Methods for managing Pain and other symptoms

Explain how often a full pain assessment needs to be done i.e.
• In- patients at least every shift
• Out-patients at every encounter
• Patients in labor, on admission, at least to understand if their pain is typical or atypical of an individual in labor and if there are other pain sites unrelated to the labor and delivery process

Discuss the requirements for reassessment of pain i.e.
• Patients with a pain score ≤ 2 or 2.5 in neonates for 24 hours should be reassessed for every shift
• Patients with pain score of 2 or more are reassessed every 4 hours
• 30-60 minutes after an implementation of an intervention for pain or more frequently as required
• Patients receiving IV pain medication with titrated dose ranges will be reassessed and documented every 10-15 minutes until the pain is relieved
• Reassessment must include frequency, duration, character, location and intensity of pain e.g. for women in labor – the frequency of contractions, the duration of the contractions and the pain score
Explain how to document pain assessment and reassessment in the patient forms and notes according to area of practice.
